Article Title: 2,800+ wolves killed, nearly $10 million spent and 15 caribou herds still at risk: Why scientists say British Columbia is targeting the wrong problem
Article Text:
A minor threat

Many wolves suffer a slow, painful death, according to information obtained by Pacific Wild.

A provincial project

Intervening in an ecosystem

By altering habitats and killing predators selectively, they affect entire ecosystems in a domino effect

Since 2015, British Columbia has killed 200-300 wolves annually to help endangered caribou populations recover. Recently, the provincial government has proposed extending its decade-long wolf cull program by five more years in areas that are home to 15 declining woodland caribou herds. But according to scientists, the deforestation, not the wolves, is the main driver of caribou declines. They claim the province's focus on wolf culls is a short-sighted approach that will ultimately not even save the caribou population but also have adverse unintended consequences on the ecosystem, according to a report by Mongabay.In April 2026, provincial authorities in the region began engaging key stakeholders about the proposed extension under its Caribou Recovery Program. They talked to about 70 First Nations in affected areas, hundreds of landowners, environmental NGOs and others. According to a spokesperson from the provincial Ministry of Water, Land and Resource Stewardship and the Ministry of Forests, they are expected to make a final decision by October.If the proposal passes, the government will continue shooting grey wolves, the primary predators of woodland caribou in 15 areas with herds.Eleven of these locations will have a yearly cull; in four, the canids will be killed every two years, said the spokesperson.B.C.’s wolf cull program was instituted to reverse historic caribou declines. Provincial data today show the ungulate’s numbers are rising in areas where wolves are killed. But the proposed extension, without steps to address habitat loss, has sparked outrage and concern among conservationists and scientists.At the Raincoast Conservation Foundation, a B.C. based NGO, wildlife biologist Paul Paquet described it as an "equivocal, intensely debated" issue. “There’s a lot of moral confusion and ethical dilemmas here on this question about protecting caribou and helping caribou by killing wolves.”Caribou do need the protection. Over the past three decades, the population of southern mountain caribou has declined by more than half and the provincial government declared about 10 herds to be locally extinct as of 2023. In 2003, the ungulates were classified as threatened under Canada’s Species at Risk Act (SARA).In 2014, the Committee on the Status of Endangered Wildlife in Canada (COSEWIC), an advisory body to the federal government on wildlife conservation, designated the caribou populations in south and central B.C. as endangered. About 1,900 caribou remain there, according to provincial estimates.Every winter, the government hires contractors to shoot entire packs of wolves from low-flying helicopters in caribou habitats, wiping out about 80-90% of these predators in the area. Many suffer a slow, painful death, according to information obtained by Pacific Wild. These killings are in addition to legalised trapping and wolf hunts in the province.But according to experts, wolves are a relatively minor threat compared to widespread loss of the caribou's preferred old-growth forest habitat, which is falling to logging and mining projects and being levelled for oil and gas pipelines.B.C.’s mountains are home to about 4,000 woodland caribou, which constitute the southern mountain population. These herds live in old-growth forests across the deep-snow regions of southeastern B.C. and parts of the northern U.S., eating lichens that grow on centuries-old trees high up the mountains to survive the winter.But over the last century, much of these old-growth forests have been cut down, harvested for timber, or levelled to make way for mining operations and oil and gas pipelines, according to a 2020 report. Loss of critical habitat starves caribou of their winter food and leaves them vulnerable to predator attacks.“Caribou’s long-term evolutionary strategy was to segregate themselves to become more of an old-growth ungulate specialist, whereas some of the other ungulates were in younger forests,” said wildlife biologist Cole Burton, who runs the Wildlife Coexistence Lab at the University of British Columbia. “So caribou could get away from some of these concentrations of wolves.”As old-growth forests fall and younger trees replace them, white-tailed deer and moose move into the landscape, Burton said, “and it’s made the conditions worse for the caribou.” Predators such as wolves, pumas, black bears and others then follow these prey species.A recent study from Burton's lab shows how clear-cut forests act as "ecological traps" for mountain caribou, who otherwise tend to avoid them. “We’ve found that the caribou in our study area are selecting these cut blocks probably because they’re nutritionally stressed,” Burton said, they’re hungry. “This is bringing them into areas where there’s more predation risk.”Apart from logging, slicing up the forest for roads and pipelines also impacts caribou. More than 600,000 kilometres (about 373,000 miles) of service roads, built to transport timber and mined ore and maintain pipelines, snake through the province, opening this terrain to humans and other animals.“Wolves use these linear features to travel two to three times faster,” said Jason Fisher, who runs the Applied Conservation Macroecology Lab at the University of Victoria, Canada, referring to his study that investigated moose deaths. “A faster wolf increases its encounter rate with caribou, which increases kill rates and draws caribou populations down.”Habitat lost to logging and fires pushes caribou closer to the brink. “What human activity has done is created more access and shifted those predator-prey dynamics,” said Greer from the Raincoast Conservation Foundation. “When [caribou numbers] get to such a low point, one wolf running into one caribou can make a huge difference.”In 2015, the B.C. government launched the predator management program, targeting wolves and pumas (Puma concolor) in key caribou habitat. “It was originally described as an emergency measure and a very short-term action to take as a kind of last-ditch effort to save some of these dwindling caribou herds,” said Kristen Weiss, wildlife and forests campaigner at Pacific Wild, a B.C.-based environmental nonprofit that’s followed the impact of the wolf culls since they began.But that “emergency measure” has continued for more than a decade, killing 200-300 wolves each year. To date, B.C. has killed about 2,800 wolves, spending about C$13 million ($9.4 million) in taxpayer money.It still remains unclear how this has affected the numbers of the wolves. The province estimates there are anywhere between 5,300 and 11,600 wolves and says it isn’t a species of concern. But no one knows for sure as there hasn’t been a B.C.-wide s ystematic survey. Wolves are intelligent animals with a highly organised social structure. “Removing breeding individuals can have huge impacts on the persistence of that pack and the longevity of that pack,” said Chelsea Greer, director of the wolf conservation program at the Raincoast Conservation Foundation, adding that by killing adults, “you’re losing a lot of generational knowledge” among packs.The last cull program, which began in 2021, expired in March of this year. Officials reached out to stakeholders for input, but unlike the last extension, they have not made a public announcement or engaged the public in discussions. “There hasn’t been a lot of clarity around the process of how they decide they’re to extend or not,” Weiss said, adding that her organisation was consulted by representatives from the caribou recovery program. “We were not given a proposal document; they just gave us a short PowerPoint presentation about their proposed extension, and then we were meant to provide feedback.”A more recent survey, conducted in 2026 by Pacific Wild, found about three-quarters of the province’s people oppose any wolf killing.As humans continue to interfere with the landscape by altering habitats and killing predators selectively, they affect entire ecosystems in a domino effect, say conservationists. While some of these effects are known, others are not.Killing large numbers of wolves from helicopters changes the behaviour of the canids, according to a 2025 study by Fisher, Burton and their colleagues. “Instead of being predominantly active during the day, they switch to nighttime mode … that’s when they come out in force, because they clearly recognise that the daytime is a dangerous place for them to be,” Fisher said. The wolves then prey on small mammals active at night, such as snowshoe hares.The study also found that coyotes and lynx, which compete with wolves, also adjusted the times when they prowl. “Before the cull, when you had wolves dominating a landscape, coyotes and lynx used patches of the landscape where wolves were not,” Fisher said. When the wolves disappeared, these other predators became more active.However, Fisher said, “We don’t know what the knock-on effects are going to be.” Coyotes can hunt and kill caribou calves. If these canids replace their larger cousins, it will mean that the wolves were killed essentially for no reason, Fisher said.Habitat restoration will take years, possibly a century before it really takes effect, wildlife biologist Fisher said, “and caribou don’t have a century.” “We have to stop the rampant development, clearing of new linear features and areas, and we have to restore what we’ve already disturbed. We have to start it now if we want to have an ecosystem that looks boreal in the next century,” Fisher said, urging the province to act now.But some short-term fixes do exist. Studies show that blocking roads and seismic lines and putting up flags near them drives wolves away. Another intervention is to turn the soil where roads and pipelines exist, mound it up, plant trees and help forests regrow, so wolves don't use the roads as shortcuts to get to the caribou.
Article Summary: Since 2015, British Columbia has killed 200-300 wolves annually to help endangered caribou populations recover. Recently, the provincial government has proposed extending its decade-long wolf cull program by five more years. But according to scientists, the deforestation, not the wolves, is the main driver ofCaribou declines. The province is expected to make a final decision by October.

Article Title: A Florida man moved $300,000 into his checking account after a caller said he had missed jury duty; his wife tracked him on Find My iPhone and a police officer stopped the wire
Article Text:
Step-by-step instructions

Protecting yourself from scams

As much as humans love to tout the AI boom and tech developments, it comes with a heavy hand of pros and cons. What we create and advance is used correctly by a set of people and adversely by others, creating a for-and-against game that involves the entire society at large. While others create a situation for people to earn money, some sit back and find ways to steal it from them.Now, a Pinellas County man is warning people after nearly thousands of dollars in a sophisticated warrant scam and demands for wired cash. Ben Wagner said he was at work when he received a call from someone posing as "Chief Hobbs" with the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office, according to a report by FOX13. The caller claimed Wagner had a warrant out for his arrest for missing a jury summons.To make the story believable, the caller even emailed a fake warrant that included Wagner's correct name, listed charges and the sheriff's name. Wagner said the details seemed legitimate and even looked up the names online while trying to verify the information. "This doesn't seem normal," Wagner said. "But again, my son was home and the last thing I wanted my son to see is dad getting handcuffed in the front yard."The scammer went on to provide Wagner with step-by-step instructions.They instructed him to drive to the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office on Ulmerton Road while keeping him under a fake gag order so he would not tell anyone. However, his wife tracked his location using Find My iPhone."Thankfully, my wife is tracking me," Wagner said. "We have Find My iPhone, and she was able to say I'm concerned about you, and I'm going to call the police, and thank got she did. The next text I got from her was, ' It's a scam."By that time, the callers had directed Wagner to transfer $300,000 to his checking account and wire the funds. A Largo police officer pulled up next to Wagner and tried to speak directly to the caller, causing the scammer to hang up.Authorities have not yet identified the suspect operating the scheme or confirmed if other local residents lost money.To avoid falling victim to scams, residents should always ask callers for a badge number and request to call back through the main department dispatch number. Ask what payment methods the agency accepts, as requests involving Zelle, gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency are major red flags.The Pinellas County Sheriff's Office noted it will never call, text or email asking for money or banking information over the phone. Anyone who receives a suspicious call should hang up immediately and contact local police using a verified number.
Article Summary: Ben Wagner said he received a call from someone posing as "Chief Hobbs" with the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office. The caller claimed Wagner had a warrant out for his arrest for missing a jury summons. The scammer went on to provide Wagner with step-by-step instructions.

Article Title: Jackie Chan became the face of a campaign to save one of the world's most trafficked mammals; his Kung Fu Pangolin campaign urged China to stop buying their scales
Article Text:
Jackie Chan took on a new fight to save pangolins

Why pangolins became one of the world's most trafficked mammals

How the Kung Fu Pangolin campaign reached China

Did Jackie Chan's campaign change attitudes towards pangolin products?

China strengthened pangolin protection after the campaign

Jackie Chan, one of China's best-known film stars, became the face of a high-profile campaign in 2017 aimed at reducing demand for pangolin products and helping protect one of the world's most trafficked mammals. The campaign, called “Kung Fu Pangolin”, used Chan's martial-arts image to deliver a simple message to consumers in China and Vietnam, where pangolin meat and scales had been in demand. In the 47-second public-service advertisement, Chan tries to teach pangolins kung fu so they can defend themselves against poachers, only to discover that the animals respond to danger by curling into protective balls. Produced by WildAid with The Nature Conservancy, the campaign urged people not to buy pangolin products and highlighted how consumer demand can fuel the illegal wildlife trade.Jackie Chan's role in the campaign was to use his enormous popularity to bring attention to an animal that was far less familiar to the public than tigers, elephants or rhinos. In the “Kung Fu Pangolin” advertisement, the martial-arts star attempts to train pangolins to defend themselves against poachers, but the animals repeatedly curl into balls when threatened. The humorous idea was built around a serious fact about pangolins.Their natural defence against predators is to roll themselves into a tight ball, but this offers little protection when humans can simply pick them up and transport them. The campaign was created by WildAid and The Nature Conservancy, with the China Wildlife Conservation Association also involved, and was designed to discourage consumers from buying pangolin meat and scales. Chan's celebrity status gave the campaign access to a mass audience and helped turn pangolin trafficking into a more visible public issue.Pangolins have been heavily targeted by illegal wildlife traders because of demand for their meat and scales. Their scales are made of keratin, the same protein found in human fingernails and hair, but they have historically been used in traditional medicine based on claims that are not supported by modern scientific evidence. Pangolin meat has also been consumed as food in some markets. The combination of these demands has made pangolins a valuable target for poachers and traffickers. All eight pangolin species are threatened, although their individual conservation classifications vary, with some listed as Critically Endangered and others as Endangered or Vulnerable on the IUCN Red List. The animals are particularly vulnerable to hunting because they are slow-moving and rely on curling into a ball rather than fleeing when confronted. Once captured, they can be transported relatively easily, making them attractive targets for illegal wildlife traders.The scale of the trade prompted international action. At the 2016 Conference of the Parties to CITES, all eight pangolin species were transferred to Appendix I, the convention's highest level of protection. The listing, which took effect in January 2017, prohibited international commercial trade in wild pangolins and their parts. However, the measure did not automatically eliminate illegal trafficking or domestic markets, making demand reduction an important part of the wider conservation response.WildAid did not rely only on the online video featuring Chan. The organisation distributed the campaign through a large outdoor advertising network in China, placing the message on more than 100,000 screens across 37 cities. Billboards and other public advertisements were also used to reinforce the campaign. WildAid reported that the campaign's social-media content generated millions of views, while donated media support helped extend its reach across major population centres. The strategy was designed to put pangolin conservation in front of ordinary consumers rather than limiting the message to wildlife enthusiasts.The campaign was part of WildAid's broader effort to reduce demand for wildlife products in China and Vietnam. Its philosophy was that stopping illegal wildlife trafficking requires more than catching poachers and intercepting shipments. If consumers continue to purchase products made from threatened animals, there remains a financial incentive to capture and transport them. WildAid therefore sought to make wildlife consumption socially undesirable while explaining the consequences for endangered species. Chan's involvement was especially useful because the campaign could use humour and his martial-arts persona to communicate the message without relying on technical conservation language.There were indications that demand-reduction campaigns were changing public perceptions, although the available evidence does not prove that the Jackie Chan advertisement alone reduced the illegal pangolin trade. WildAid reported that the proportion of surveyed Chinese respondents who believed pangolin scales had medicinal value fell from 70% in 2015 to 50% in 2017, around the period when its pangolin demand-reduction campaign was being conducted. The organisation also commissioned research into reactions to the Jackie Chan advertisement, with respondents reporting that the PSA made them less likely to purchase pangolin products. These findings are useful evidence of changing attitudes, but they measure perceptions and self-reported intentions rather than actual purchases or trafficking volumes.That distinction is important when assessing celebrity conservation campaigns. A successful advertisement can raise awareness and make consumers reconsider their behaviour, but it cannot by itself stop poaching networks or guarantee that wildlife products disappear from illegal markets. Pangolin conservation requires enforcement, habitat protection, international cooperation and long-term reductions in consumer demand. Chan's contribution was therefore primarily in communication and public engagement rather than direct wildlife protection.The campaign formed part of a broader period of change in pangolin conservation. China strengthened its domestic protection of pangolins in 2020, when all pangolin species in the country were upgraded from second-class to first-class nationally protected wild animals. The move provided the animals with stronger legal protection and reflected growing concern over their conservation status and illegal exploitation. China also introduced additional measures aimed at restricting the use and trade of pangolin products.The international and domestic measures complemented campaigns aimed at changing consumer behaviour. CITES restrictions addressed international commercial trade, Chinese law strengthened domestic protection, and organisations such as WildAid worked to reduce demand. Together, these approaches recognised that trafficking cannot be addressed effectively through enforcement alone if there is still a market for the products.Pangolins, meanwhile, remain under pressure despite these interventions. Illegal trafficking continues to pose a major threat, and seizures of pangolin scales have been reported in different parts of the world even after international trade restrictions were strengthened. Conservationists therefore continue to emphasise the need for enforcement, protection of wild populations and sustained efforts to discourage people from buying pangolin products. Chan's campaign did not end the trade, but it helped bring the issue to a much larger audience.The lasting significance of “Kung Fu Pangolin” is the way it turned a complicated wildlife-trafficking problem into an easily understood message. Jackie Chan did not single-handedly save the pangolin, nor can the campaign be credited with ending the illegal trade. Its value was in using one of China's most recognisable celebrities to challenge the perceived value of pangolin products and connect consumer choices with the survival of a threatened group of mammals. The campaign showed how celebrity influence can complement scientific research, international agreements and government enforcement by tackling another critical part of the problem, the demand that keeps illegal wildlife markets profitable.
Article Summary: Jackie Chan became the face of a campaign to reduce demand for pangolin products. The campaign, called ‘Kung Fu Pangolin’, used Chan's martial-arts image to deliver a simple message. In the 47-second public-service advertisement, Chan tries to teach pangolins kung fu so they can defend themselves against poachers.

Article Title: Mike Tyson started keeping pigeons as a bullied Brooklyn boy, finding love and comfort in them; decades later, he still has hundreds of birds across the US
Article Text:
Mike Tyson's connection with pigeons began in Brooklyn

One pigeon became connected to his first fight

Pigeons remained with him as boxing took over

Tyson treated pigeon racing almost like another form of competition

His collection has been much larger than a normal backyard flock

Tyson still has hundreds of pigeons decades later

From Brooklyn rooftops to birds across America

Long before Mike Tyson became one of boxing's most feared heavyweight champions, pigeons were a source of love and comfort for him. Tyson has recalled being bullied as a child growing up in Brooklyn and finding refuge in the pigeons he kept, saying that spending time with them helped take his mind off the world around him and the people who picked on him. The birds became so important that Tyson later described pigeons as the first loving relationship he ever had. They were also unexpectedly connected to the beginning of his fighting life. Tyson has said that when a neighbourhood bully killed one of his pigeons in front of him, he fought back, marking what he has described as his first fight. More than five decades later, his fascination with the birds remains strong. In March 2025, Tyson said he owned hundreds of pigeons, perhaps as many as 1,000, across the US.Tyson's relationship with pigeons goes back to his childhood in Brooklyn, where he became involved with the birds long before he entered boxing. His affection for them developed at a time when he was dealing with difficulties at home and being bullied by other children. In a 2011 New Yorker account, Tyson explained that spending time with pigeons helped take his mind away from the world he was living in and the people who bullied him.The birds gave him something to care for and a space where he could escape from the pressures around him. Tyson has also recalled that he was around 11 when pigeons became closely connected with his life and eventual involvement in fighting.Tyson's attachment to pigeons was unusually deep for a childhood hobby. He has described them as his first loving relationship, a phrase that captures how emotionally important the birds became to him. His interest was not simply about owning animals. He spent time caring for them, watching them fly and becoming familiar with the different types of pigeons and their behaviour. The rooftop pigeon coops of Brooklyn became a place where he could spend time away from the difficulties of his childhood. The New Yorker reported Tyson explaining that the birds helped him take his mind off the world around him, particularly the people who bullied him.Perhaps the most remarkable part of Tyson's pigeon story is the connection he has drawn between the birds and his development as a fighter. According to accounts of Tyson's childhood, a neighbourhood bully took one of his pigeons, killed it and threw the bird at Tyson. Tyson reacted by punching the boy. CBS reported in 2011 that Tyson's first punch came after a neighbourhood bully killed one of his beloved pigeons. Tyson has repeatedly told versions of this story and has connected the incident with the beginning of his fighting instinct. It should be treated as Tyson's own account of an important moment in his life, rather than as proof that the incident alone caused his boxing career.As Tyson's life changed and he rose through the boxing world, his relationship with pigeons did not disappear. He continued keeping birds even after becoming heavyweight champion and one of the most recognisable athletes in the world. The New Yorker reported in 2011 that Tyson had raised pigeons before he began boxing, while earlier reporting documented his continued involvement with pigeon keeping in adulthood. The contrast was striking. Outside the ring Tyson became known for extraordinary power and aggression, yet around his pigeons he displayed a markedly gentler side. One account described him gently kissing a pigeon on the beak before releasing it, highlighting how different his relationship with the birds could look from his public image as a fighter.Tyson eventually took his lifelong interest further by becoming involved in competitive homing-pigeon racing. In 2011, Animal Planet's six-part series Taking on Tyson followed the former heavyweight champion as he attempted to build a team and compete in the sport. CBS reported that Tyson was a longtime pigeon fancier but a novice at racing, with experienced racers helping him learn the competitive side of the hobby. Homing-pigeon racing involves releasing birds away from their home lofts and timing how quickly they return. The races can progress from relatively short distances to hundreds of miles.The competitive element appealed to Tyson because it gave him another form of challenge after years in boxing. His involvement was not limited to watching birds fly. He learned about breeding, training and preparing pigeons for races and worked with experienced people in the sport. The 2011 series showed Tyson moving into a world that was unfamiliar to him despite his lifelong experience with pigeons. His passion also attracted controversy. Animal rights organisation PETA criticised his involvement in pigeon racing, arguing that racing could expose birds to injuries, exhaustion and other risks. Tyson's supporters and people involved in the sport, meanwhile, presented it as an established competitive tradition centred on the birds' homing ability.Tyson's pigeon collection has varied considerably in size over the years, and figures reported at different times should not be treated as a single permanent total. In 2011, The New Yorker reported that Tyson had around 3,000 birds, while other contemporary accounts also put his collection in the thousands. At other points, reports focused on much smaller numbers kept at particular homes. These differences are important because Tyson has maintained birds in different locations and because the size of a racing or breeding collection can change over time. What is clear is that his involvement has extended far beyond keeping a handful of pet pigeons.The most useful current figure comes directly from Tyson himself. In a March 2025 interview with PEOPLE, the then-58-year-old Tyson said he owned hundreds of pigeons, adding that the total could be “maybe a thousand”. He said the birds were spread across California, New Jersey, Florida and Las Vegas. This is the strongest basis for saying that Tyson still keeps hundreds of pigeons across the US. Because the figure is Tyson's own estimate rather than an independently verified count, it is more accurate to report it as hundreds, possibly around 1,000, rather than stating that he definitely owns exactly 1,000 birds.Tyson's latest comments make clear that pigeons are not simply a nostalgic reminder of his childhood. He told PEOPLE that he has been involved with pigeons for longer than he has done anything else, including boxing. He also said that pigeons had both got him into trouble and got him out of trouble and described them as something that had been part of his entire life. His remark that boxing is over but pigeons are still here neatly captures the unusual longevity of the relationship. The heavyweight championship years came and went, but the birds remained a constant presence.The geography of Tyson's pigeon keeping has changed dramatically since his childhood. What began with birds around Brooklyn's rooftops eventually became a passion involving lofts and birds in different parts of the country. His 2025 account places pigeons in California, New Jersey, Florida and Las Vegas, showing that the hobby has followed him through several stages of his adult life. Yet the basic attraction appears unchanged. Tyson still photographs and makes videos with his birds and has even included them in promotional material. For someone whose public identity was built around violence and competition, his decades-long devotion to pigeons offers a very different picture of the man away from the boxing ring.
Article Summary: Mike Tyson's relationship with pigeons goes back to his childhood in Brooklyn. His affection for them developed at a time when he was dealing with difficulties at home and being bullied by other children. Tyson has said that when a neighbourhood bully killed one of his pigeons in front of him, he fought back, marking what he has described as his first fight.

Article Title: In 2003, crews began removing non-native fish from the Grand Canyon; by 2006 rainbow trout’s share of the catch had fallen from about 90% to under 10%
Article Text:
Why were the fish being removed?

More than 36,500 fish were caught

Native fish appeared to benefit but scientists couldn’t take all the credit

The battle did not end in 2006

In the depths of the Grand Canyon, scientists were trying to give native fish a better chance of survival, by taking other fish out of the Colorado River. A four-year fish-removal experiment conducted between 2003 and 2006 dramatically changed the composition of fish being caught in one section of the river. According to a 2011 study by Michael D. Coggins Jr., Michael D. Yard and William E. Pine III, published in Transactions of the American Fisheries Society and available through the U.S. Geological Survey, rainbow trout went from making up about 90% of the catch at the beginning of the experiment to less than 10% by August 2006. But the story was more complicated than simply removing an invasive species and watching native fish return.The target was the federally protected humpback chub, a native fish of the Colorado River that had faced major ecological pressures. The humpback chub is specially adapted to the warm, sediment-rich and fast-flowing waters that historically characterized the river. After the construction of Glen Canyon Dam, the river’s conditions changed substantially, including becoming colder and clearer in many areas. Those changes helped create conditions in which introduced trout could thrive.Rainbow and brown trout can prey on native fish, including humpback chub, while also competing with them for resources. The National Park Service identifies invasive fish as one of the continuing challenges facing native fish populations in the Grand Canyon. So researchers set out to test whether reducing the number of non-native fish could improve conditions for native species.During the 2003–2006 experiment, crews captured more than 36,500 fish belonging to 15 species in the mechanical-removal reach. About 64% of the total catch was made up of non-native fish. Rainbow trout alone accounted for 19,020 fish, followed by fathead minnows, common carp and brown trout.Native fish made up the remaining 36%, including more than 7,300 flannelmouth suckers, 2,600 humpback chub, 2,200 bluehead suckers and more than 1,000 speckled dace. The change in the catch was striking. Rainbow trout’s contribution fell steadily from approximately 90% in January 2003 to below 10% in August 2006. The overall share of non-native fish also fell sharply, from more than 95% at the beginning of the experiment to below 50% after July 2005.The researchers also observed an increase in juvenile native fish within the removal area, suggesting that reducing non-native fish may have improved native fish survival and recruitment. Yet the scientists were careful about claiming a straightforward cause-and-effect victory.During the same period, drought increased river temperatures, while rainbow trout abundance was declining across the wider river system. Those simultaneous changes made it difficult to determine exactly how much of the improvement in native fish recruitment came from the removal program itself and how much resulted from changing environmental conditions. That uncertainty is reflected in the study’s title: Nonnative fish control in the Colorado River in Grand Canyon, Arizona: An effective program or serendipitous timing?The experiment became part of a much larger effort to protect the Grand Canyon’s native fish. Today, the National Park Service continues to control invasive trout in parts of the Colorado River system, including through electrofishing and trapping. Its conservation work also includes moving humpback chub into suitable tributaries and monitoring native fish populations.The humpback chub itself has since been downlisted from endangered to threatened status, but it remains a conservation priority. Grand Canyon National Park contains the largest remaining population of the species. The 2003–2006 experiment therefore offers a revealing lesson in conservation: removing a non-native predator can rapidly reshape an ecosystem, but nature rarely provides a single explanation for what happens next. In the Grand Canyon, the falling numbers of rainbow trout coincided with other environmental changes, leaving scientists to disentangle how much was deliberate intervention and how much was timing.
Article Summary: A four-year fish-removal experiment conducted between 2003 and 2006 dramatically changed the composition of fish being caught in one section of the Colorado River. Rainbow trout went from making up about 90% of the catch at the beginning of the experiment to less than 10% by August 2006. But the story was more complicated than simply removing an invasive species and watching native fish return.

Article Title: Two Amazon delivery drivers carried an 85-year-old Kentucky woman’s printer inside; minutes later she stopped breathing and they performed CPR that helped save her life
Article Text:
The woman's son thanked Eric and Shawn for saving his mother's life. (AI enhanced image)

Drivers respond quickly

Son says help came in time

Drivers plan to return

Amazon praises

An ordinary delivery turned into a medical emergency for two Amazon delivery drivers in Covington, Kentucky, on Tuesday. Eric Bunzow and Shawn Beam had just delivered a printer to an 85-year-old woman when she suddenly collapsed.According to Fox 19, Bunzow and Beam, who are longtime friends and Amazon Delivery Service Partner drivers, had carried the printer inside the woman’s home. After the delivery, she invited them to see the view from her balcony. Few moments later, she said she was feeling dizzy.“She said, ‘Oh, you ain’t seen nothing, let’s go look at the balcony,’” Bunzow said. “As we were walking, she said, ‘Young man, I feel a little dizzy.’ I said, ‘Here, hold my hand, I’ll set you down.’ When she grabbed my hand, she collapsed.”The woman fell into Beam, who helped prevent her from hitting her head. The two drivers then realised that she was not breathing and immediately began responding to the emergency.Beam, who has training in safety response, began the Heimlich manoeuvre after the woman collapsed. At the same time, Bunzow called paramedics for help.“I said, ‘Eric, she’s not breathing.’ He said, ‘What?’ I said, ‘She’s not breathing!’” Beam reacalled.Bunzow said he recognised the symptoms because of a previous experience. The emergency also reminded him of the death of his mother, who died in March.“My mom passed away in March, and then to watch her ... she died on us ... like he said, we were at the right place at the right time,” Bunzow said.The drivers continued helping the woman while waiting for emergency responders. Paramedics arrived within five minutes.The woman’s son, James, said the actions of the two drivers may have made a major difference because they were already inside the home when his mother collapsed.He said emergency responders might not have arrived in time without Bunzow and Beam being there and acting quickly.“The fact they were there and made quick actions- we’re not planning a funeral,” James said. “We are celebrating my mom being around for more time.”Bunzow and Beam said they plan to visit the 85-year-old woman again. They remembered the balcony and the view she had wanted to show them before the emergency. “Eventually, we want to see that view and make sure that she’s doing okay,” Bunzow said.Beam also said he hoped they could return and spend some time with her on the patio. “Just sit on the patio with her and be like, ‘Look at this, amazing,’” Beam said. “I bet there’s a nice breeze coming through there right now.”Amazon said Bunzow and Beam’s actions reflected the response and care expected from its Delivery Service Partner community.“We’re proud of Eric and Shawn for their courage and quick response in helping a resident experiencing a medical emergency while they were out on their delivery route,” Amazon said in a statement.The company said the two drivers deliver for a Delivery Service Partner in its network and described their actions as an example of drivers supporting the communities they serve.“Eric and Shawn deliver for a Delivery Service Partner in our network, and their actions reflect the compassion and character we see across the DSP community, where drivers regularly go above and beyond to support the communities they serve,” Amazon said.The company also said its thoughts were with the woman and her family as she continued her recovery.
Article Summary: Eric Bunzow and Shawn Beam had just delivered a printer to an 85-year-old woman when she suddenly collapsed. The woman fell into Beam, who helped prevent her from hitting her head. The two drivers then realised that she was not breathing and immediately began responding to the emergency.

Article Title: Colorado farmer Marc Arnusch turned down solar leases on 2,700 acres; instead he chose a conservation easement to protect the family farm, then faced an IRS audit
Article Text: Colorado farmer Marc Arnusch had a straightforward choice: accept millions of dollars from solar companies seeking to lease 2,700 acres of his family’s farmland, or keep the property in agriculture for the next generation. He chose the farm. Now, after spending nearly $1 million documenting a conservation easement, he is facing an IRS audit over the tax deduction associated with it. Reporting by Just the News, recent statements from the Internal Revenue Service and reporting by Colorado Public Radio help illuminate the dispute and the broader debate over conservation easements. Arnusch, a third-generation farmer in Weld County, said the solar offers were tempting but ultimately incompatible with what he wanted for the land.Instead, his family pursued a conservation easement, a legal agreement that permanently limits certain uses of privately owned land in order to protect its conservation values. Federal law allows qualifying conservation easements to generate charitable tax deductions, provided the statutory requirements are met.The decision required extensive documentation. Arnusch’s family hired roughly a dozen specialists, including tax attorneys, engineers, solar experts, mineral geologists and land-use professionals.Soil testing, core samples, zoning and boundary surveys and other studies were used to establish what is known as the property’s “highest and best use”, an appraisal concept that considers the most valuable use that is legally permissible, physically possible and financially feasible.The solar companies’ interest in the property was part of that equation. Their offers provided evidence that solar development could represent a significant economic use of the land. An independent appraisal was then prepared using the information gathered by the family’s experts. Arnusch claimed a tax deduction based on the resulting valuation, although he says he has not yet been able to use the full deduction because he did not have sufficient income.Then, roughly three years after the deduction was claimed, the IRS opened an audit. According to Arnusch, an IRS employee visited the farm, and he questioned whether the person conducting the review had the expertise necessary to evaluate such a complicated property.Arnusch said the family had relied on numerous experts throughout the process, but the IRS later sent an auditor who, according to Arnusch, was conducting their first audit of a farm. The IRS did not respond to requests for comment.Arnusch’s experience is part of a much larger fight over conservation-easement valuations. Critics of the IRS’s approach argue that government reviews can reach dramatically lower valuations than those produced by taxpayers who commission extensive expert studies.Bernie Donachie, a value-analytics specialist with interests in conservation-easement properties, examined 10 publicly available cases. He found that taxpayers’ experts had collectively valued the properties at $358.2 million, while IRS valuations totaled about $1.57 million, a reduction of roughly 99 percent, according to his analysis reported by Just the News. Those figures represent Donachie’s sample, not an official governmentwide assessment.The controversy comes against the backdrop of years of IRS enforcement involving conservation easements. The agency has argued that legitimate conservation deductions should be protected while abusive transactions and inflated valuations should not receive tax benefits. Now, the IRS is changing how it handles the issue.On Aug. 19, the agency announced the creation of an Office of Conservation Easements, saying the new office will centralize technical expertise and coordinate policy, enforcement and case-resolution strategies involving conservation and historic-preservation easements. The IRS simultaneously ended its current uniform settlement initiative, saying standardized settlement letters were not suited to the variety of cases it was handling.For taxpayers with pending cases, the change does not automatically mean their disputes will disappear. The IRS says they can continue seeking settlements through their assigned examination or Chief Counsel representatives, with individual cases potentially resolved on different terms depending on the circumstances and litigation risks.For Arnusch, however, the issue is more personal than a dispute over a tax bill. He chose conservation because he wanted his family’s land to remain a farm rather than become a solar development. Now he is waiting to see whether the government will accept the valuation that helped him make that choice.He does not want to keep fighting the government; he simply wants to protect the farm. For a family that has spent generations working the same ground, the question is whether preserving that future will ultimately come with a tax price they cannot afford.
Article Summary: Colorado farmer Marc Arnusch had a straightforward choice: accept millions of dollars from solar companies seeking to lease 2,700 acres of his family’s farmland, or keep the property in agriculture. He chose the farm. Now, after spending nearly $1 million documenting a conservation easement, he is facing an IRS audit over the tax deduction associated with it.

Article Title: US Pentagon issues guidelines for testosterone screening for troops aged 30 and above
Article Text:
Under the guidance issued on Wednesday, all male service members aged 30 and older will undergo mandatory blood tests to measure testosterone levels. Men under 30 will be tested only if they request it or if doctors identify warning signs.

The US Pentagon has issued clinical guidelines for mandatory testosterone deficiency screening of active-duty and reserve service members aged 30 and above, with the new policy taking effect immediately, as the Defence Department seeks to identify hormonal and energy-related issues that could affect military readiness.Under the guidance issued on Wednesday, all male service members aged 30 and older will undergo mandatory blood tests to measure testosterone levels. Men under 30 will be tested only if they request it or if doctors identify warning signs.The policy follows Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement in July that the military would introduce testosterone screening. Hegseth has repeatedly promoted testosterone use, prompting questions from medical experts about the scientific basis for broad screening.The new guidance also sets out separate screening and treatment pathways for women. Routine testosterone blood tests will not be mandatory for female service members. Instead, doctors are instructed to screen for symptoms such as fatigue and disrupted menstrual cycles.These symptoms can be linked to hormonal problems and conditions known as low-energy availability and relative energy deficiency in sport.The Pentagon has also provided guidance on when doctors may prescribe testosterone to women for uses not specifically approved by regulators.This includes postmenopausal women with unusually low sexual desire.For men, the guidelines set out pathways for evaluating and treating low testosterone after screening. The Pentagon says the approach is intended to identify and manage conditions that could affect energy, health and readiness.However, the policy has drawn concern from doctors and other experts. They have questioned whether widespread testing could result in unnecessary or potentially harmful testosterone treatment.There is also limited evidence that routinely screening military personnel for low testosterone would improve combat readiness, experts have said.The US Food and Drug Administration is expected to hold a meeting of experts in mid-September to discuss the medical use of testosterone, adding to the scrutiny surrounding the Pentagon's new policy.
Article Summary: All male service members aged 30 and older will undergo mandatory blood tests to measure testosterone levels. Men under 30 will be tested only if they request it or if doctors identify warning signs. The policy follows Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's announcement in July that the military would introduce testosterone screening.

Article Title: Two injured in explosion at railway station in Germany’s Augsburg
Article Text:
The station has been completely shut down and rail services suspended (File photo)

Two people sustained minor injuries after an unidentified object exploded at a train station in the southern German city of Augsburg, local media reported.Window panes were also damaged in the explosion, which occurred in a passageway inside the station.Police responded to the incident at around 5 am local time and cordoned off parts of the station as officers investigated the scene. An explosive-disposal robot was also deployed.The station was later completely shut down and rail services were suspended after police described the object as “suspicious”, without providing further details. Earlier, one track had remained operational.Augsburg is a regional transport hub located around 55 km (35 miles) west of Munich, Germany’s third-largest city after capital Berlin and Hamburg.
Article Summary: Window panes were also damaged in the explosion, which occurred in a passageway inside the station. The station was later completely shut down and rail services were suspended. Police described the object as ‘suspicious’, without providing further details.

Article Title: Pennsylvania police shooting: Officer charged in death of college student
Article Text:
A Pennsylvania police officer has been charged with voluntary manslaughter after shooting and killing a 22-year-old college student.

A Pennsylvania police officer has been charged with voluntary manslaughter after shooting and killing a 22-year-old college student who had wound up at the incorrect residence late at night while waiting for friends to pick him up, stated by the prosecutor on Tuesday.Upper Pottsgrove Police Cpl. Sean Farrell, 58, is accused of Glenwood Earl Pysher IV's death in August 23, according to Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele. The officer did not have to kill Pysher during the confrontation since officer had less-lethal choices, according to the prosecuter.According to a news statement from the district attorney's office, the Montgomery County Detective Bureau looked into the shooting and examined video from Farrell's body-worn camera.According to the inquiry, "Cpl. Farrell had a taser and other less-lethal weapons on his utility belt that he did not use. The victim had his hands raised and was not carrying a weapon at the time of the shot, and the officer was safely behind a vehicle from Pysher. There was no danger from Mr. Pysher. This is not a legal use of deadly force, leading to the charge of Voluntary Manslaughter," as per the news release from Steele.Pysher's family lawyer thanked the prosecution in a statement.Attorney Ken Fulginiti stated, "The family is grateful for the work of the Montgomery County District Attorney's office and they are looking forward to justice in this horribly tragic, preventable, and reckless conduct that took their son's life."On Tuesday, Farrell surrendered to the Montgomery County Detectives. According to a district attorney's office representative, Farrell must surrender all firearms to the state police in order to be released after Magisterial District Judge Kathleen Rebar set bail at $75,000. On September 10, he will have a preliminary hearing.When a resident contacted 911 to report someone attempting to break into a home through the rear door, Farrell was the first officer on the scene. According to the statement, Farrell's body-worn video captured the officer moving down the driveway with his gun drawn and illuminating the path with its light.Farrell noticed Pysher on the patio of the house, close to the back door, while standing behind a car in the driveway. "Police, let me see your hands," shouted Farrell. "Hands up, hands up now, drop to the ground," he then shouted.According to the statement, Pysher was seen on camera raising his hands as he started to approach the officer and kept going in that way as the officer ordered, "Drop to the ground." "Drop to the ground," Farrell yelled once more, followed by "Stop or I'll..." However, according to the district attorney's office, Farrell fired two rounds before he could complete the sentence, striking Pysher twice in the chest.According to the announcement, Pysher was shot between 17 and 20 feet (5 and 6 meters) away from the officer.Pysher had been out at many pubs earlier in the evening to celebrate a friend's 21st birthday, according to the inquiry. Around 11 p.m., a designated driver took the party to the birthday person's house. About 30 minutes later, Pysher exited to walk half a mile to another friend's house to continue drinking, but he ended up at the incorrect residence, according to the release. Based on what his son's friends have told him, Pysher's father has stated that he thinks his son attempted to enter what he believed to be his friend's home.Glen Pysher told The Associated Press last week that "his son tried to open the doorknob and obviously startled the homeowner." According to what we know, he said, "He believed he was at his friend's house, so he said, "Hey! Open the door!"The father said that after his son sat down on the back porch and called his buddies, they noticed he was in the wrong area and started looking for him.Philip Stinson, a criminal justice professor at Bowling Green State University, maintains a national database of almost 25,000 police officer arrests since 2005.Stinson's research shows that between January 2005 and the end of July 2026, 218 local sworn police officers were charged with either murder or manslaughter in a fatal police shot that occurred while they were on duty. Although there are still a number of unresolved cases, 78 policemen have been found guilty, while 107 have been found not guilty or discharged.During that period, ten cops in Pennsylvania were accused, six of them were found guilty.According to Stinson, there have been variations in the number of cops charged over time, but those variations are statistically minor considering that there are about a thousand fatal police confrontations annually."These are ugly situations. "The facts are never simple," Stinson said. Criminal juries and grand juries appear to have similar problems. In a potentially violent street confrontation, they are hesitant to question the split-second, frequently life-or-death judgments made by an on-duty police officer.Most cops involved in deadly on-duty shootings shot an unarmed victim. Just ten of the victims in the 78 convictions had guns when they were shot.
Article Summary: Upper Pottsgrove Police Cpl. Sean Farrell, 58, is accused of Glenwood Earl Pysher IV's death in August 23, according to Montgomery County District Attorney Kevin Steele. Farrell had a taser and other less-lethal weapons on his utility belt that he did not use.

Article Title: In 2017, USGS injected 13.5 liters of red dye into Ohio’s Sandusky River during a grass carp spawning event; downstream stations measured dye movement
Article Text:
An AI-generated image showing researchers releasing red tracer dye into Ohio’s Sandusky River to measure how material drifting in the current moves downstream during grass carp spawning research. Credits - Google Gemini

Why a river needed to be dyed at all

Watching red water pass a string of stations

An AI-generated image showing scientists monitoring the Sandusky River downstream after a red dye tracer was released to study water movement and help model the drift of grass carp eggs. Credits - ChatGPT

Turning drift times into a map of where carp spawn

Some invasive species are easy to track because they leave visible damage behind, such as stripped vegetation or a collapsed food web that points investigators to the culprit. Grass carp are harder to track because they spawn by releasing eggs directly into moving water rather than building a nest researchers can easily locate and observe. Scientists working on Ohio's Sandusky River needed a way around that problem. On 11 July 2017, USGS researchers injected 13.5 litres of Rhodamine WT dye into the Sandusky River at the Tiffin Road bridge crossing. The timing was deliberate. A grass carp spawning event was already underway downstream, and scientists from the US Geological Survey wanted to know how far and how fast a fish egg would drift once it entered the water. Those measurements could then be used to improve models of where grass carp eggs were likely to have originated.Grass carp are not native to the Sandusky River or anywhere in the Great Lakes basin. The species was brought to the United States in the 1960s to control aquatic vegetation, and escaped populations later established themselves in the Mississippi River system before spreading toward Lake Erie.Spawning was first confirmed in the Sandusky River in 2015, when researchers collected fertilised eggs drifting downstream, and further surveys in the years that followed documented repeated spawning events in the same stretch of river. That confirmation mattered because fertilised grass carp eggs behave in a specific way once they are released. Rather than sinking or sticking to the riverbed, they remain suspended in the current as they drift and develop, so their fate depends largely on how the water is moving. That single fact, that eggs travel much like any other object caught in the current, is what made a dye tracer study worth running in the first place.Rhodamine WT, the dye used in the study, is a bright red compound that fluoresces under the right light and can be measured at very low concentrations, making it useful for tracing how quickly water moves through a river system. According to a USGS data release, the dye was injected near the Tiffin Road bridge crossing, and its concentration was then recorded at fixed monitoring stations downstream over the following two days, alongside water velocity and discharge readings taken from survey boats stationed on the river. Because the dye moved with the river current, the data showed how quickly material entering the river near a suspected spawning site would reach each downstream sampling point and how that timing varied with flow. Matching the dye data against the eggs researchers found in their nets was the next step, and it is where the study's value emerged.Ichthyoplankton nets at multiple sites along the lower Sandusky River had already collected thousands of grass carp eggs on several dates in 2017. Pairing that catch data with the dye study allowed scientists to work backward from where an egg was caught to roughly where and when it was spawned. A related USGS publication describes using drift modelling to estimate a likely spawning location several kilometres downstream of Ballville Dam. In June 2018, researchers collected fertilised eggs and adult grass carp within that model-predicted spawning area, confirming the location and validating the modelling approach. The dye tracer study filled that gap by using coloured water and careful timing. The approach has since become a template for tracking other river-spawning species whose eggs, like grass carp eggs, drift rather than stay put.
Article Summary: US Geological Survey researchers injected 13.5 litres of Rhodamine WT dye into the Sandusky River at the Tiffin Road bridge crossing. A grass carp spawning event was already underway downstream, and scientists from the US Geological Survey wanted to know how far and how fast a fish egg would drift once it entered the water.

Article Title: In 2021, South Carolina sank a retired 250-foot barge off Edisto Island; its water tower and containers now give snapper and grouper cave-like shelter
Article Text:
An AI generated image showing underwater view of a commercial barge moving through a river, illustrating the hidden activity and water movement beneath the surface. Credits - Google Gemini

A partnership behind the scrap pile

Why shape matters more than size to a fish

Swamp Sculpture - Edisto Island. Credits - Wikimedia Commons

A layered habitat built over decades

Much of South Carolina’s seafloor is flat and sandy, offering little shelter for fish along the coast. For decades, the state’s wildlife managers have tried to change that by sinking retired ships, vehicles and construction debris to give marine life places to cling to and hide. One of their more elaborate efforts came in September 2021, when a 250-foot decommissioned barge was towed about 10 nautical miles off Edisto Island and deliberately sunk. On its deck were sections of a dismantled municipal water tower, a dozen shipping containers with holes cut through their steel walls, and a life-sized concrete sculpture of a great white shark. It took approximately two hours for the barge to disappear beneath the waves. Five years later, the structure remains part of the Edisto 60-foot artificial reef, where its containers and water-tower sections provide the varied shelter the project was designed to create for marine lifeThe project was led by the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, whose artificial reef programme has spent decades building habitat along a coastline short of hard, rocky seafloor. According to SCDNR , the barge and its cargo were contributed through a partnership with the Coastal Conservation Association of South Carolina and Sea Hunt Boat Company, which together funded half the cost of the barge and its tow to the reef site. The water tower sections came from Mount Pleasant, which had recently demolished an old municipal tank and donated the steel instead of scrapping it. For the Coastal Conservation Association, the Edisto deployment marked its fifteenth reef contribution in the state, part of a longer-running effort to keep adding material to South Carolina's permitted reef sites.Robert Martore, the programme’s long-time head, explained that the key factor was shelter, not size.According to the South Carolina Department of Natural Resources, the open spaces inside the shipping containers create a cave-like interior that larger species such as snapper and grouper prefer, while the flatter pieces of the water tower provide low-relief refuge for smaller and juvenile fish. That mix of structure sizes is deliberate. A stretch of open sand offers almost nothing for a young fish to hide behind, so even modest variation in height and enclosure can draw in a wider range of species than a single uniform shape would. That same logic, giving fish a reason to stay rather than simply pass through, is the entire premise behind building artificial reefs at all.The barge did not create a reef so much as add to an existing one. Known as the Edisto 60-foot reef, or PA 30, the site lies about 10 nautical miles offshore and had already received more than 20 structures before 2021, including a large ship, decommissioned military vehicles and rubble salvaged from the old Cooper River Bridge. According to NOAA Fisheries , artificial reefs work by providing new or enhanced hard-bottom habitat in areas that would otherwise be habitat-limited, giving space for organisms to colonise quickly and offering juvenile fish more places to shelter from predators. Along much of South Carolina's coast, where the natural seafloor is largely flat and sandy, that kind of added structure can make an outsized difference to how much marine life an area supports.For anglers and divers, the appeal is immediate. A reef with this variety of structure can provide habitat for snapper, grouper and other reef-associated species, turning otherwise open seafloor into a more complex fishing and diving site. Species such as red snapper and gag grouper are slow to mature and tend to stay close to the structure they settle near, which is why fisheries managers pay close attention to where new reef material is placed. There is also a concrete shark at one end of the wreck, a detail that has nothing to do with fish biology. Programme staff built the sculpture themselves as something divers would enjoy photographing, a small acknowledgement that an artificial reef is meant to be visited as well as inhabited.
Article Summary: South Carolina's artificial reef programme has spent decades building habitat along a coastline short of hard, rocky seafloor. One of their more elaborate efforts came in September 2021, when a 250-foot decommissioned barge was towed about 10 nautical miles off Edisto Island and deliberately sunk. On its deck were sections of a dismantled municipal water tower, a dozen shipping containers with holes cut through their steel walls, and a life-sized concrete shark.

Article Title: 'They can't go to the bathroom': Trump claims US has eyes on Iran’s every move
Article Text:
Trump said Iran had been attempting to rebuild radar systems and missile capabilities in the region. He claimed US surveillance had detected preparations for a rocket designed to deploy mines in the waterway.

US President Donald Trump has said that the US has “very strong control” over the Strait of Hormuz and is closely monitoring Iran’s military activity in the strategic waterway. He claimed American forces detected and destroyed a rocket system being developed to lay mines.Addressing the press about the situation in Iran, Trump said that US forces had also removed mines from the strait and were continuing to move oil tankers through the key shipping route."We've controlled, and we are controlling the Hormuz Strait. We are bringing lots of boats out every day with millions of barrels of oil. We are, for the most part, doing it without trouble."Trump said Iran had been attempting to rebuild radar systems and missile capabilities in the region. He claimed US surveillance had detected preparations for a rocket designed to deploy mines in the waterway."They were trying to rebuild their radar systems and a missile system and a mine drop. You know, we got rid of all the mines in the Hormuz Strait."According to Trump, the US identified the rocket system before it became operational and struck it while construction was nearing completion."They were building it. It was almost finished, so we took it out.We saw that they were building it. We see everything that they're doing."Trump also claimed that US forces had targeted other Iranian military assets. He portrayed American surveillance capabilities as extensive enough to track Iran's movements in near real time."They can't move. They can't go to the bathroom without us seeing it. So we saw that. We took it out. We took out some other things..."He said US forces had faced limited resistance while operating around the strait. Trump claimed that Iranian forces occasionally fired drones, but said American forces had been able to intercept them."Every once in a while, they shoot a drone and we knock it down. But we have control, very strong control."The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial global oil shipping route. Any disruption there can affect energy supplies and international oil markets, making control of the waterway a major strategic issue in the US-Iran confrontation.
Article Summary: Trump said Iran had been attempting to rebuild radar systems and missile capabilities in the region. He claimed US surveillance had detected preparations for a rocket designed to deploy mines in the waterway. The Strait of Hormuz is a crucial global oil shipping route. Any disruption there can affect energy supplies and international oil markets.

Article Title: In the 1940s, Seabiscuit retired to a California ranch; decades later its redwoods, oak woodlands and wetlands became a conservation priority
Article Text:
​George Woolf on Seabiscuit (Image: Wikipedia)

Seabiscuit found a quiet retirement at Ridgewood Ranch

Seabiscuit found a quiet retirement at Ridgewood Ranch/ Seabiscuit with owner Charles Howard (Wikipedia)

From a famous horse ranch to a landscape worth protecting

More than 4,600 acres became part of a conservation effort

A living monument to Seabiscuit and California wildlife

For years, Ridgewood Ranch in Mendocino County, California, was known primarily as the place where Seabiscuit, one of America’s most famous racehorses, spent his retirement. After a remarkable racing career, the champion arrived at the ranch in 1940, where he lived until his death in 1947. But the property’s importance extends far beyond its connection to a legendary horse. Its rolling oak woodlands, redwood forests, streams, wetlands and working farmland have also made it an important landscape for wildlife and conservation. In the early 2000s, preservationists and landowners were working to protect more than 4,600 acres of the remaining ranch from development. Today, Ridgewood continues to carry both its historic and environmental legacy, with conservation easements protecting important habitats and historic structures preserving the memory of Seabiscuit and the Howard family.Seabiscuit’s final chapter unfolded at Ridgewood Ranch, where his stud barn was completed in 1940, marking the beginning of the property’s period of historic significance. According to the National Register of Historic Places, the barn is locally significant for its association with Seabiscuit and his owner, Charles S. Howard, and for its connection to entertainment and recreation. Although the races that established Seabiscuit’s international reputation had already taken place, his retirement at Ridgewood turned the remote Mendocino County ranch into an unexpected tourist attraction.Racing fans travelled in large numbers to see the celebrated horse during his final years, with thousands of visitors making the journey to the ranch. The stud barn was also part of Howard’s working horse operation, rather than simply a monument to a retired champion. Seabiscuit remained there until his death in 1947, aged 14, bringing the barn’s recognised period of significance to a close.The story of Ridgewood Ranch did not end with Seabiscuit’s death. After the Howard era, the property changed hands, eventually coming under the ownership of Christ’s Church of the Golden Rule. The ranch had once covered roughly 16,000 acres, although substantial portions were sold over the years. By the early 2000s, conservationists were increasingly concerned that development and subdivision could threaten what remained. Ridgewood was not simply valuable because of its connection to Seabiscuit; it was also a working agricultural landscape containing forests, grazing land, streams and wetlands. The Seabiscuit Heritage Foundation says its broader preservation mission includes protecting the remaining ranch landscape and its cultural legacy. In 2004, the National Trust for Historic Preservation named Ridgewood one of America’s 11 Most Endangered Historic Places, drawing further attention to the need for long-term protection.The push to preserve Ridgewood gained momentum through partnerships involving the landowners, the Mendocino Land Trust and other conservation organisations. At the time, plans called for more than 4,600 acres of the remaining ranch to be placed under permanent conservation protection, safeguarding open space and working farmland from development. The conservation effort eventually produced specific easements covering important portions of the landscape. The Mendocino Land Trust says it now holds two conservation easements at Ridgewood, one protecting 33 acres of old-growth and large second-growth redwoods, and another permanently protecting 1,689 acres of oak woodland habitat. The Seabiscuit Heritage Foundation also records protected streams, tributaries, riparian habitat and wetlands across the ranch. These measures mean Ridgewood’s value is no longer limited to its historical association with a famous racehorse; parts of the landscape are protected because they provide important ecological and wildlife habitat.Today, Ridgewood Ranch represents an unusual meeting point between sporting history, working agriculture and environmental conservation. Its protected habitats include oak woodlands, redwoods, rangeland, seasonal wetlands and waterways that support species such as steelhead, golden eagles, great blue herons, bears, mountain lions, foxes, deer and yellow-legged frogs. Seabiscuit’s legacy is preserved alongside that natural environment. His stud barn, where he spent his retirement years, was restored and added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2014. The ranch remains a working landscape rather than a conventional museum, while visitors can learn about its history through tours and preserved buildings. In this way, the land that once offered Seabiscuit a peaceful final chapter has become something larger, a place where a celebrated sporting story and a valuable California ecosystem continue to survive together.
Article Summary: Ridgewood Ranch in Mendocino County, California, was known primarily as the place where Seabiscuit, one of America’s most famous racehorses, spent his retirement. After a remarkable racing career, the champion arrived at the ranch in 1940, where he lived until his death in 1947. Its rolling oak woodlands, redwood forests, streams, wetlands and working farmland have also made it an important landscape for wildlife and conservation.

Article Title: In 1932, stressed shoe salesman I.W. Stevens followed his doctor’s advice and bought a 400-acre Minnesota island; nearly 50 years of diaries now survive in Voyageurs National Park
Article Text:
Voyageurs National Park. Image credits: NPS

From lumber-company retreat to summer resort

I.W. Stevens' resort near Namakan Lake. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

From a resort owner to self-sufficient islander

A life preserved in Voyageurs National Park

Ingvald Walter “I.W.” Stevens purchased a 400-acre island in what is now Voyageurs National Park in 1932. Stevens had been a shoe salesman in Hibbing, Minnesota, but after stress-related health issues and advice from his doctor, he moved toward the solitude of Namakan Lake. In the beginning, he ran a summer resort in the area and later lived year-round on the island, eventually living there for nearly 50 years.Born in Vang, Valdres, Norway, in 1885, Stevens later immigrated to the United States at the age of 19, and in 1918, he moved to Hibbing, where he became a shoe salesman. Stevens’s own account that is preserved by the National Park Service says that in 1932 he became interested in buying lakeshore property in Minnesota, prompting him to venture out that summer to scout available tracts across Namakan Lake.In 1905, Edward Hines founded the Virginia and Rainy Lake Lumber Company, whose retreat was located on what was then known as Williams Island, now called Stevens Island. Although the company’s timber operations logged large stands of trees somewhere else, Hines preserved the island’s red and white pines and used the property to entertain lumber buyers. In 1929, when pine logging ended, Edward Hines put his land holdings on sale.Three years later, I.W. Stevens bought the island with the intention of establishing a summer resort.Stevens, in his own records, wrote that following surgery for haemorrhaging stomach ulcers in March 1932, he used his convalescence to reevaluate his high-stress career. This prompted him to submit his resignation as manager of the Ladies’ Shoe Department at the Itasca Department Store.Shifting his life's direction, he spent two weeks camping around Kabetogama Lake in August 1932 before reaching Namakan Lake, where he learned that the Virginia and Rainy Lake Lumber Company was selling parcels. He later reportedly returned with a company representative and quickly became interested in the former headquarters and decided to purchase it.After his move to the island, Stevens started working on his original plan to turn the property into a summer resort; he spent several years preparing the landscape for his ambition. In 1937, Pine Cove Resort welcomed its first paying guests.The NPS reported that Stevens harvested ice, cut wood, painted boats and cleaned cabins for guests; but at the age of 74 in 1959, he gave up the demanding business. From then on, the island ceased its commercial operations and became primarily his home, where his daily activities focused on providing for himself.The former shoe salesman grew vegetables, picked and canned blueberries, ground wheat and baked bread, caught fish and hunted deer, while also gathering wood for cooking and heating. Though his life was highly independent, it was not completely cut off from other people. The NPS has noted that over the years, Stevens entertained many family members and friends. He also became a writer, contributing articles to outdoor magazines and maintaining a daily diary as he documented his life around Namakan Lake. Eventually, at the age of 94, he left Namakan Lake. Stevens died in 1990 at the age of 104, more than five decades after his move to northern Minnesota.Today, Stevens Island is considered one of the 13 visitor destination sites in Voyageurs National Park. The site preserves structures from the resort era of the 1930s, including Stevens’ cabin, a guest cabin, sauna, woodshop and root cellar. These structures remain to tell part of Stevens’ story. His writings provide a personal perspective of his transition from a Hibbing shoe salesman to a resort operator. While his stay on the island lasted nearly five decades, his own account specifically records 42 years of diaries, thus making those journals a detailed window into the life he led near Namakan Lake.
Article Summary: I.W. Stevens purchased a 400-acre island in what is now Voyageurs National Park in 1932. Stevens had been a shoe salesman in Hibbing, Minnesota, but after stress-related health issues and advice from his doctor, he moved toward the solitude of Namakan Lake. In the beginning, he ran a summer resort in the area and later lived year-round on the island.

Article Title: In June 1998, the US Army turned 13,000 pounds of mixed plastic into a 25-foot Fort Leonard Wood bridge designed to carry light vehicles across a creek
Article Text:
Representative Image: An AI-generated conceptual rendering illustrating a U.S. Army light vehicle crossing a 25-foot tactical bridge engineered from recycled thermoplastic lumber at Fort Leonard Wood. Credits: ChatGPT

Transformation from mixed waste to a bridge material

Military exercise at Fort Leonard Wood. Image credits: Wikimedia Commons

A bridge made out of recycled-plastic lumber for vehicles

Why the Army wanted to use mixed plastic

The US Army finished an unusual project in June 1998 at Fort Leonard Wood, Missouri, routing around 13,000 pounds of recovered mixed plastic that would have likely ended up in a landfill. The 25-foot-long structure was made across the creek at Gammon Field and was designed to carry loads equivalent to light vehicles. The US Army Construction Engineering Research Laboratories (CERL), alongside Fort Leonard Wood’s Directorate of Public Works, led this project.Engineers did not build the entire structure out of plastic, though. The recycled-plastic components were installed as the primary spanning superstructure directly onto the six steel beams that had supported the original wooden bridge.
