15 newborns died after a fire broke out in the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences (PIMS) in Islamabad on Wednesday.According to PIMS officials, the nursery housed 16 newborns when the fire broke out, with only one baby rescued from the ward, reported local outlet Geo News. The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue officials.The blaze broke out at around 7 am in the gynaecology ward of the hospital on the third floor of the MCH ward, in Pakistan's federal capital. Rescue teams were deployed to the hospital and worked to extinguish the fire and evacuate those inside while carrying out cooling operations at the site.According to the district administration, 14 of the 15 children killed were completely burnt.The incident has raised concerns over safety measures in the hospital's neonatal and maternity facilities.Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident and directed authorities to identify those responsible and take strict action. He expressed deep grief over the deaths, saying that a tragedy involving children was an “irreparable loss”, and said he shared the grief of the bereaved parents.The Prime Minister also directed authorities to conduct a detailed review of fire-safety arrangements and the factors that contributed to the incident, with the aim of preventing similar tragedies in hospitals.Meanwhile, an inquiry committee headed by the additional deputy commissioner general has also been formed to determine how the fire started and establish responsibility. The blaze broke out in the hospital’s gynaecology ward, where the nursery was located.
Article Summary: 15 newborns died after a fire broke out in the gynaecology ward of the Pakistan Institute of Medical Sciences in Islamabad. The fire reportedly started after an air-conditioner compressor exploded inside the nursery, according to rescue sources. Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has ordered an immediate investigation into the incident.

Article Title: Five labourers gunned down at construction site in Pakistan's Balochistan
Article Text: Five labourers from Pakistan’s Punjab province were shot dead at a construction site in Balochistan’s Pishin district, a provincial government official said Tuesday, according to news agency PTI.The labourers were killed by unidentified gunmen in Saranan town on Monday morning, Balochistan government spokesperson Shahid Rind said. Their bodies were sent to their hometowns in Punjab for burial.Arrangements were made to transport the bodies to their respective villages in Ahmedpur Sharqia and Bahawalpur, Rind said. Security forces have launched a search operation to track down the attackers.Balochistan chief minister Sarfaraz Bugti condemned the killings and vowed action against those responsible."Those shedding the blood of innocent laborers deserve no leniency," Bugti said in a statement issued by his office. "The cowardly acts of terrorists cannot weaken the provincial government's resolve."Saranan town has witnessed militant attacks since last week. A few days ago, gunmen attacked a police station in the town and fled with weapons, ammunition and two vehicles.Banned Baloch insurgent groups have frequently targeted workers and labourers from other provinces working in Balochistan.In July, five barbers from Multan were shot dead in Mashkail town after armed men on motorcycles opened fire at their barber shop.Last month, six labourers from Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa were abducted in the Nasirabad area of Turbat district. Their bullet-riddled bodies were later found in a remote area, police said.Security and law enforcement agencies have been conducting a large-scale operation against insurgent groups in parts of Balochistan since early July. However, the attacks have continued.In a separate incident on Sunday, five policemen were injured when two unidentified men hurled a hand grenade at a police post in Ambar tehsil of Mohmand district in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa.Police retaliated with gunfire, forcing the attackers to flee. The injured policemen were taken to a nearby hospital and are said to be out of danger. An investigation is underway.Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, which borders Afghanistan, has witnessed recurring militant violence, including attacks linked to insurgent groups, cross-border movement of fighters and repeated military operations.
Article Summary: The labourers were killed by unidentified gunmen in Saranan town on Monday morning. Security forces have launched a search operation to track down the attackers. Baloch insurgent groups have frequently targeted workers and labourers from other provinces working in Balochistan. In July, five barbers from Multan were shot dead in Mashkail town.

Article Title: Pakistan army officer pulls gun, fires in air amid student protest at Peshawar university- video
Article Text:
Sarhad University, Peshawar, Pakistan (Picture from X)

A Pakistan army officer opened fire into the air during a student protest at Sarhad University in Peshawar, triggering chaos and a scuffle on the campus, according to local media reports and videos circulating online.The incident comes amid growing unrest in Pakistan, with protests and demonstrations also being reported from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and Balochistan, adding to the challenges facing the country's military and political establishment.According to reports, the officer, said to be a colonel, was the husband of a faculty member at Sarhad University. He reportedly got into a heated confrontation with protesting students, which soon escalated into a physical scuffle.Videos shared by several social media accounts purportedly show the officer striking students with a stick amid the confrontation. As tensions escalated, he allegedly pulled out a pistol and initially pointed it towards the protesters before raising the weapon in the air.The officer was then seen firing shots into the air, sparking panic and further uproar on the university campus.Reports said the officer has been taken into custody, while the Pakistan army has ordered an inquiry into the incident.
Article Summary: Pakistan army officer opened fire during student protest at Sarhad University. Incident triggered chaos and a scuffle on the campus, according to reports. Incident comes amid growing unrest in Pakistan, with protests and demonstrations also being reported from Pakistan-occupied Kashmir and Balochistan.

Article Title: 97-yr-old survives 8-9 hrs in debris, gives hope for more miracles
Article Text:
Residents pull a newly installed zipline to help people commute across the Trishuli river in the aftermath of flash floods at Bidur in Nepal's Nuwakot district, Nepal.

TRISHULI BAZAAR: Two two-year-old girls and a 97-year-old woman emerged at opposite ends of the age spectrum among survivors of Nepal’s Aug 26 flood, which tore through the Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor, sweeping away homes, schools, roads and bridges. The toddlers were listed as safe in Nepal govt’s survivor database, while the elderly woman survived after spending around eight to nine hours trapped in mud and debris. Their stories have given the embattled country hope that it desperately needs.Sabya Munakami (2) was recorded as found safe at Devighat in Bidur Municipality-3 on Aug 27, a day after floodwaters swept downstream into Nuwakot. The official record did not detail where she was when the flood struck, who was with her or how she managed to remain safe. Another two-year-old girl, Kabya Munakami, made it out safely at Devighat.On the other side was Guna Maya Bohara (97) the oldest documented survivor verified after the disaster. Floodwater, mud and debris engulfed the care home where she was staying at Kabilash in Nuwakot, leaving her trapped as roads disappeared and rescuers struggled to reach the area.Her grandson Rasik Bohra said she had been stuck in the mud for around eight to nine hours when relatives spotted a small movement.“She was shaking her head,” he said. That movement told the family she was still alive.Rescuers and relatives worked through dense mud and wreckage for several hours to free her. Heavy machinery cleared a route through the devastated area as ambulances were unable to reach the spot.Once Bohara was freed, rescuers placed her in the large metal bucket of an earthmover and carried her across. Her clothes, hair and face were covered in sludge as she sat silently in the bucket on the way to safety. “I was emotional. I can’t express that feeling,” Rasik said. Her great-nephew Dipak Bohara, who had travelled from Kathmandu and joined the rescue effort, described the 97-year-old as looking like “a warrior” returning from battle after she was pulled out alive.Bohara was later taken to Bir Hospital in Kathmandu. Despite her age and the hours she spent trapped, she suffered no significant injuries. “Nothing happened to her. She is totally fine now,” Rasik said. “She was very strong. At that age... it’s a wonder.”The family’s relief was, however, tempered by the continuing search for relatives and others missing. Rasik said the scale of destruction made it difficult to know how many remained unaccounted for. “There are so many people like me who are stuck,” he said.China restores access to Tibet disaster zone: China has fully reopened the only road leading to the Gyirong border crossing into Nepal a week after sections were washed away, allowing heavy machinery to reach the main disaster zone for the first time. The damage to the G216 national highway had meant that China had been airdropping supplies to frontline rescuers.
Article Summary: Sabya Munakami (2) was recorded as found safe at Devighat in Bidur Municipality-3 on Aug 27, a day after floodwaters swept downstream into Nuwakot. Guna Maya Bohara (97) is the oldest documented survivor verified after the disaster.

Article Title: Economy in disaster-hit zone blooms, but locals feel left out
Article Text:
Some visitors paid premium rates even to stay in partially damaged houses

TRISHULI BAZAAR: A disaster-linked service economy has sprung up across Trishuli Bazaar, Bidur and Dhunche after the Aug 26 flash floods, as journalists from across the world, aid workers, engineers, insurance and loss assessors and families searching for missing relatives crowded the broken Bhote Koshi-Trishuli corridor, filling available rooms and sharply driving up the cost of transport, shelter and local "assistance".Hoteliers in Trishuli Bazaar and settlements further north told TOI they had received more guests in the past week than they had seen in the previous four to five years. Hotels, guesthouses and homestays on higher and relatively safer ground filled first, with several operators saying rooms were booked soon after international teams began arriving.As regular accommodation ran out, demand spilled into lower-lying areas where residents still feared another flood. Some visitors paid premium rates even to stay in partially damaged houses, while others took whatever space was available despite concerns over the river and further rain. "People are paying premium rates to sleep on the floor in the lower bazaar, even with the river still running dangerously high," a guesthouse owner in Bidur said on condition of anonymity.The squeeze has extended to transport. With bridges washed away and roads badly damaged, movement through several stretches is now restricted to jeeps and 4x4 vehicles capable of negotiating mud, broken roads, steep approaches and risky detours.Residents said "businessmen" are not differentiating between families looking for loved ones who are missing and those who have trooped in for work. "A jeep driver asked for a month's wages just for a ride across a damaged ridge," said a local man in Trishuli Bazaar who was searching for his sister. "The outsiders take all the vehicles because they have the budget. We are left walking in the mud."Demand also surged for bilingual translators, guides and fixers familiar with the terrain, villages and local administration. They help visiting teams locate relief camps, arrange vehicles and passes, secure village access, establish contacts and organise and translate interviews.Local guides and fixers said that international media organisations were paying as much as $150 a day for people who could navigate difficult access routes. "A foreign network paid me over $100 just to get them past the blockades and translate interviews at a shelter," a fixer in Dhunche said. "I am making more in a day than I usually make in a month, but the result is that many local people are left out in the cold."
Article Summary: Hoteliers in Trishuli Bazaar and settlements further north said they had received more guests in the past week than they had seen in the previous four to five years. Hotels, guesthouses and homestays on higher and relatively safer ground filled first. Some visitors paid premium rates even to stay in partially damaged houses.

Article Title: A week on, Nepal moves to rehab as hopes of finding survivors fade
Article Text:
Nepal has shifted its focus from rescue to relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction

TRISHULI BAZAAR (NEPAL): Govt in Nepal has shifted its focus from rescue to relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction a week after the Aug 26 Bhote Koshi flood as hopes of finding survivors across most of the devastated corridor recede. Search teams, however, continued digging into hydropower tunnels where workers could still be alive in chambers or air pockets.Nepal Police Wednesday put the toll at 1,127 dead and 4,858 missing. For Indian families, uncertainty continued: New Delhi's last detailed missing-person update listed 275 nationals and 128 persons of Indian origin, or PIOs, as missing or uncontactable. India subsequently said 163 of its nationals had been rescued in Nepal, but did not issue a revised missing count. Across the border in Tibet, Chinese authorities raised the toll to 21 dead and 541 missing. The missing there included 49 Indians. The Tibet figure was compiled separately and could overlap with India's list of missing nationals.Prime Minister Balendra Shah announced the change in govt's priorities after days dominated by frantic searches for survivors.Rescue teams already on the ground, though, haven't abandoned search.Police uploaded details of 911 unidentified bodies to help families searching for relatives.Govt is now focusing on rehabilitation while working to protect the lives of people in the affected areas and providing the necessary medical treatment and psychological counselling,” Shah said. The change in emphasis came as the possibility of live rescues diminished sharply outside a few hydropower sites.Binoj Basnet, a retired senior army general who oversaw rescue operations during Nepal’s 2015 earthquake, said, “Looking at the nature of the disaster and the area which has been hit by the flood, as days go by there are less chances of human survivors.”Rescue teams on the ground, though, haven’t abandoned search. Their strongest remaining hope centres on hydropower tunnels in Rasuwa, where workers may have reached rooms or sections containing air pockets and access to water. Hundreds of people linked to hydropower projects are unaccounted for.Nepal had explored drilling or excavating into the tunnels from above rather than relying only on entrances blocked by thick slurry, rocks and debris. Heavy rain repeatedly complicated these operations, with water entering some tunnels and machinery struggling to reach project sites.Indian specialists were among teams working at the tunnel sites. India sent a specialised tunnel rescue team and technical experts to Nepal, while a 19-member forensic team worked in Kathmandu to help identify bodies through DNA and other methods.Shah told parliament Wednesday that govt had mobilised security forces, helicopters, medical teams and relief supplies immediately after receiving information about the disaster. He also thanked India and China for their assistance, including technical support. India’s role remained particularly significant because hundreds of Indians were caught on both sides of the Nepal-Tibet border when the flood struck.
Article Summary: Nepal has shifted its focus from rescue to relief, rehabilitation and reconstruction. Search teams continued digging into hydropower tunnels where workers could still be alive in chambers or air pockets. Prime Minister Balendra Shah announced the change in govt's priorities after days dominated by frantic searches for survivors.
